Class TrackingDifferentiator

java.lang.Object
yams.core.math.TrackingDifferentiator
public class TrackingDifferentiator extends Object
Tracking differentiator.

Written by FRC Team 8331, who contributed active disturbance rejection control to YAMS.

A tracking differentiator turns a raw reference into a smooth reference y together with its first and second derivatives yd and ydd. Feeding the smoothed reference to a controller avoids the large output spikes that a step setpoint would otherwise produce: the controller follows a trajectory the mechanism can actually track instead of demanding an instantaneous change.

Mechanisms rarely construct this class directly; they configure one through ADRCConfig.withTrackingDifferentiator(Method, double...) and the controller applies it to every setpoint.

The methods

Five discrete implementations are supported, selected with TrackingDifferentiator.Method. Each takes a small list of double parameters; any parameter may be omitted by passing a shorter array (or null), and the default documented below is used instead.

TrackingDifferentiator.Method.EULER: exponential smoothing

The mildest option: a first-order low-pass filter on the reference. One parameter:

  • alpha in [0, 1], default 0.9, the smoothing factor. Higher smooths more and follows slower; lower tracks the raw reference more closely.

Its time constant is about dt / (1 - alpha), so it changes with the sample time, and its yd jumps to (1 - alpha) * step / dt on a step. Use when the reference needs only gentle rounding.

TrackingDifferentiator.Method.TOD: time-optimal tracking

Bang-bang: full acceleration toward the reference, then full braking. One parameter:

  • r greater than 0, default 1.0, the acceleration bound in the loop's units per second squared; higher tracks faster.

Its sign switching makes yd chatter by about 2 * r * dt at rest, and a large r never settles at a 20 ms period. Use it only with a short sample time.

TrackingDifferentiator.Method.LD: linear differentiator

A linear second-order filter with critically damped-style poles. One parameter:

  • lambda greater than 0, default 1.0, the time constant of the filter in seconds. The sample period must stay below 2 * lambda or the filter is unstable.

Smooth and predictable, with no overshoot: a step is followed to 98% in about 5.8 * lambda, at a peak rate of about step / (e * lambda). The best default.

TrackingDifferentiator.Method.RED: nonlinear reduced differentiator

A super-twisting filter that converges in finite time. Two parameters:

  • lambda1 greater than 0, default 1.0, the gain on the square root of the error; how hard the error pulls.
  • lambda2 greater than 0, default 1.0, the gain on the sign of the error; the bound on how quickly yd changes, in the loop's units per second squared.

It overshoots a step, and like TrackingDifferentiator.Method.TOD its sign switching makes yd chatter at rest at a 20 ms period.

TrackingDifferentiator.Method.INTD: integral differentiator

A saturating second-order filter, ydd = -r^2 * beta / (1 - alpha) * tanh((1 - alpha) * (y - ref) / gamma) - r * yd. Far from the reference it cruises at r * beta / (1 - alpha); near it, it lands like TrackingDifferentiator.Method.LD with natural frequency r * sqrt(beta / gamma) and damping 0.5 * sqrt(gamma / beta). Four parameters:

  • alpha in [0, 1), default 0.5, widens the linear region and raises the cruise speed.
  • beta greater than 0, default 1.0, in the loop's units, sets the cruise speed.
  • gamma greater than 0, default 1.0, in the loop's units, the width of the linear region; 4 * beta gives critical damping, smaller overshoots.
  • r greater than 0, default 1.0, per second, the speed of the dynamics.

Useful when step sizes vary a lot: big moves cruise at a speed the mechanism can hold, small ones still land quickly. Its defaults overshoot.

Invalid parameters throw IllegalArgumentException.

Example

TrackingDifferentiator td =
    new TrackingDifferentiator(TrackingDifferentiator.Method.LD, 0.02, Optional.of(new double[] {0.08}));
td.update(setpoint);
double smoothSetpoint = td.getY();
double setpointVelocity = td.getYd();
